near_misses.why_not: Identical triggers, different questions and lines: TOOL-01 asks 'Does the hunk import or reference an external package that neither the importing module's manifest nor a manifest it inherits declares in any dependency section?' of an added import; TOOL-08 asks 'Does the change delete the last use of a package while the ecosystem's manifest still declares it as a direct dependency?' and quotes 'the deleted import line'.

Disjoint by TOOL-01's Limits: 'A declaration in any of the manifest's dependency sections (runtime, development, optional, peer or bundled) counts as declared ...; whether development-only dependencies are used by non-development code is a separate check', which is TOOL-02's 'Does a file that ships import a package that the manifest declares only in a list the shipped install leaves out?'

One added manifest entry dispatches all six, but each asks its own question: no lower bound above zero (TOOL-03), one admitted version or a tight cap in a published library (TOOL-04), a lock file that disagrees (TOOL-06), a resolved version under an advisory (TOOL-09), a trivial package that brings packages of its own (TOOL-10), a name the registry does not publish or that imitates a popular one (TOOL-11).

Different questions (TOOL-14: whether 'a rewrite or the tool's safe automatic fix would remove' the finding; TOOL-15: whether a site-specific reason is written) that share one clause (TOOL-14: 'for a temporary suppression directive, no recorded follow-up task stated'; TOOL-15: 'when marked temporary, lack a reference to its follow-up task or issue'); the spans differ (TOOL-14 quotes 'the suppression directive or placeholder and the line it silences', TOOL-15 the directive alone), so a DEFER_TO entry could not fire.

A bare directive draws both on one line, but TOOL-15 asks for a reason and TOOL-18 for a named diagnostic; the right fix carries both, as TOOL-18's own good half does: `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any -- sender defines the payload shape`.

A bare file-wide directive: TOOL-18 asks whether it names a diagnostic, TOOL-19 whether it sits wider than the element holding the findings; TOOL-19 quotes the directive 'with the element it attaches to', a different span.

An added `#[allow(x)]` whose lint no longer fires draws both on one span, but TOOL-20 asks whether the diagnostic fires at head and TOOL-21 whether the silent form was chosen; the fixes conflict ('the same code with the suppression removed' vs 'the same suppression rewritten in the self-reporting form'), and TOOL-21's is wrong there because on a lint that is not emitted 'the unfulfilled_lint_expectations lint triggers on the expect attribute', so a tiebreak, if wanted, runs 'TOOL-21' → 'TOOL-20'.

A module-level `warnings.simplefilter("ignore")` in test configuration matches both, but TOOL-16 asks whether the relaxation hides a diagnostic of the change's own code and TOOL-19 whether the filter wraps only the triggering call; TOOL-16's Limits put 'an inline suppression of a single construct' outside it.

Under a configured no-disabled-tests rule both flag an added skip mark, but TOOL-17's Limits yield to that rule ('A project that enforces a lint rule against any disabled test holds the stricter position, and there the fix is the check itself'), so TOOL-13's finding is the one to keep and no TOOL-13 → TOOL-17 entry is wanted.
An unused-dependency diagnostic (rustc unused_crate_dependencies, deptry DEP002) lands on the manifest or crate root, while TOOL-08 quotes 'the deleted import line of the package'; different spans.

near_misses.b: TOOL-02, TOOL-14, TOOL-19, TOOL-33, TOOL-36, TOOL-40, TOOL-41, TOOL-42
near_misses.why_not: Each shares a defect with TOOL-13 when the project configures the rule its Source cites (deptry DEP004; ban-ts-comment; eslint-comments disable-enable-pair; Error Prone DefaultCharset 'listed in ENABLED_WARNINGS'; ESLint no-misleading-character-class 'recommended: true'; SetTextI18n 'Do not build messages by concatenating text chunks'; Error Prone StringCaseLocaleUsage; CA1304/CA1305), but the aggregator keys a span on file, symbol and verbatim code, and these Finding outputs quote two elements ('the import line and the manifest entry', 'the suppression directive or placeholder and the line it silences', 'with the element it attaches to') or a call or expression, not TOOL-13's 'the line that draws the diagnostic'; a DEFER_TO entry fires only once the code fields agree.

A late read such as `let dir = env::var("DUMP_DIR").unwrap();` in an error path draws both on one line, but TOOL-23 asks where the read sits and TOOL-28 when the value is first parsed and checked; the fixes converge (read at start-up, pass the value down), TOOL-28's adding the check.

An option effective only with another: TOOL-27 asks whether the gating option is stated in help, documentation, a message or the name, TOOL-31 whether setting it while disabled is reported; the spans differ (the declaration vs 'the conditional read of the dependent setting'), and a TOOL-31 warning also meets TOOL-27's 'log message for an ignored one'.

Disjoint reactions to one bad value: TOOL-29 flags how initialization ends (crash, uncaught exception, silent exit, a message naming neither setting nor value), TOOL-30 a conversion that accepts the value or a default that replaces it.

Split by position: TOOL-33 asks about conversions 'at a file, socket, pipe or process boundary', TOOL-35 about bytes passed 'between the program's own routines'; a decode right after a read is the edge TOOL-35 asks for.

A concatenated literal at a display call draws both, but TOOL-39 asks whether the text bypasses the catalog and TOOL-40 whether the message is assembled from pieces; TOOL-40's fix (one catalog format string) contains TOOL-39's, and the spans differ (the display line vs 'the concatenation, interpolation or count test').

Partitioned by destination, each Limits naming the other: TOOL-41 'Numbers and dates displayed in a user interface take culture-sensitive formatting ...; that display is outside the rule'; TOOL-42 'A value that will be stored and accessed by software ... takes a locale-independent (root) form instead'.

TOOL-41's own bad line `const row = `${total.toLocaleString()},${due.toLocaleDateString()}`;` also dispatches TOOL-43 through `[.]toLocale(String|DateString|TimeString)\(`, but TOOL-41 asks about the locale of stored text and TOOL-43 about a recorded moment turned into fields with the host's zone; the spans differ (a call vs 'the line').

Partitioned by kind of value, each Limits naming the other: TOOL-43 'a future or recurring event set at a wall-clock time in a place keeps its time zone'; TOOL-44 'Records of events that have already occurred are outside the rule'.
Code vs test: TOOL-36 judges the unit of the code's own count; TOOL-37's Limits 'A slice that the test code itself takes, to build an input or to check a result, is not code under test'.
Natural-language text vs identifiers: TOOL-38's Limits 'Identifiers and syntactic content ... are matched by the rule their format defines, by default with no case folding and no normalization'.
One new option, two questions: whether it should exist at all (an internal detail or a value the program can obtain) vs whether it states range, unit, default and gating option.

contradictions.sentence_a: Each warning the change would add is fixed in the code or, when it is a false positive, marked as a false positive in the source. (Thesis)
contradictions.sentence_b: For a check that flags likely-wrong code or a matter of style, fixing remains the typical response, and a suppression comment that states its reason is an accepted outcome. A suppression directive added as a temporary measure for a pressing issue is acceptable only with a recorded follow-up task to address the underlying problem. (Limits)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A suppression the change adds with its reason stated, for a style or likely-wrong finding or as a temporary measure with a recorded follow-up task, also addresses a diagnostic that is not a false positive; whether that suppression is warranted is judged on its own.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: `#[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation, reason = "value < MAX_ITEMS fits in u32")]` and `#[allow(dead_code, reason = "temporary until issue 123 deletes it")]`, both matched by TOOL-21's trigger `#!?\[allow\(`.
contradictions.sentence_b: Where the suppression mechanism offers a form that reports itself when the suppressed diagnostic is no longer emitted, a suppression added by a change uses that form instead of the silent one. (Thesis)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: The rule judges the reason a suppression carries, not its form; where the language offers a self-reporting suppression, the reason goes in that form's reason slot.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: `#[expect(dead_code, reason = "kept for v1 readers until they migrate")]`.
contradictions.sentence_b: If that text marks the suppression as temporary (temporary, for now, until, workaround, TODO, FIXME), look in it for a reference to a task or issue. (Validator, applying the Thesis: 'A suppression added as a temporary measure to address a pressing issue also names the follow-up task or issue that addresses the underlying problem.')
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: The reason a self-reporting suppression carries meets the requirements on any suppression's reason, so a reason that marks it as temporary also names its follow-up task or issue.

contradictions.sentence_a: `fix` = that line reading the value from an environment variable, a flag or a configuration-file key, in the file's language (Finding output); the good half reads `serviceURL := os.Getenv("SERVICE_URL")` beside `resp, err := http.Get(serviceURL)`.
contradictions.sentence_b: General-purpose code is configured through explicit function arguments or structure fields rather than by reaching through to the command line or the environment, so importing it defines no flag. (Thesis)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Where the value is read is a separate concern: code outside the entry point and the one configuration module receives it as an argument or field, and the entry point or that module reads and checks it at start-up from the environment, a flag or a configuration file.

contradictions.sentence_a: A switch read from the environment at run time complies when the production deployment leaves it off. (Limits; good half `const server = createServer({ debug: process.env.APP_DEBUG === "true" });`, which TOOL-23's trigger `\bprocess[.]env\b` matches)
contradictions.sentence_b: Does the hunk add a flag definition outside the entry point; an environment or program-argument read outside the entry point, a helper in its own module that only it calls, and the one configuration module; ...? (Validator question)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Where the switch is read is a separate concern: code outside the entry point and the one configuration module receives the switch's value as an argument or field.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: `const server = createServer({ debug: process.env.APP_DEBUG === "true" });`, which TOOL-30's first trigger matches.
contradictions.sentence_b: Grep the hunk for conversions of a value read from the environment, a flag or a configuration file: ... boolean conversions that compare against one word or take the string's truth value (Validator); 'a parser that treats a boolean as off whenever it is not set to "on" turns "yes" and "enable" into off' (Rationale)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Off applies when the switch is unset; a value that is set is parsed by a conversion that rejects an unrecognised word with an error rather than reading it as off.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: `raw = os.environ.get("PORT")` and `port = 8080 if raw is None else int(raw)`, under the Thesis 'a value the parser or a check of its allowed values rejects reaches the user as an error'; PORT=80a ends in an uncaught ValueError whose message names the value but not the setting.
contradictions.sentence_b: Does a setting read in this file, when its value fails conversion or a check during initialization, end the program in a crash, a hang, an uncaught exception or panic with a stack trace, an exit before the error reaches the entry point, an exit with no message or a zero status, or a message that names neither the setting with its value nor where it was set? (Validator question)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: How a rejected value reaches the user is a separate check, a message naming the setting and its value reported at the entry point rather than an uncaught exception; this rule asks only that a present malformed value is neither accepted nor replaced.

contradictions.sentence_a: Where decoding with the host's own encoding is the intent, the call names the locale encoding explicitly. (Thesis; the Validator adds 'A call that names the locale encoding passes where the data is in the host's encoding' and the fix 'or with the locale encoding named where the host's encoding is intended')
contradictions.sentence_b: Text written into a protocol, file format or export format that a change introduces, or into an existing format that the change deploys in a new context, is encoded as UTF-8 exclusively, not as UTF-16, a code page or the host's default encoding (Thesis); its Validator greps for 'the host's default charset passed by name'.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Text that a change writes into a format it introduces, or deploys in a new context, is encoded as UTF-8; the locale encoding is named only for data that already exists in the host's encoding.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: `secret = args.password_file.read_text().strip()` and `subprocess.run(["client", "--password-stdin"], input=secret, text=True, check=True)`, both matched by TOOL-33's trigger.
contradictions.sentence_b: Does a call that converts between bytes and text at a file, socket, pipe or process boundary leave its encoding unnamed while a supported runtime version takes that call's default from the host's locale, or convert the data with an encoding other than the one it has? (Validator question; its Source: 'Python will enable UTF-8 mode by default from Python 3.15', and its Validator treats such a version 'as supported when no minimum is declared')
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: The rule concerns only the channel that carries the secret; how the program decodes the file or stream it reads the secret from is judged on its own.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: `Path(".gitignore").write_text("\n".join(ignored) + "\n")`, matched by TOOL-33's trigger `write_text\(`.
contradictions.sentence_b: Does a call that converts between bytes and text at a file, socket, pipe or process boundary leave its encoding unnamed while a supported runtime version takes that call's default from the host's locale, or convert the data with an encoding other than the one it has? (Validator question)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: The rule concerns what the ignore list and the package-manager settings name; how a script writes those files is judged on its own.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: an IllegalArgumentException message built with '+' from "APP_PORT=", the raw value and " (environment) is not 1-65535; set e.g. APP_PORT=8080", printed by `System.err.println("configuration error: " + e.getMessage());`; the Rationale addresses users left 'clueless and forced to report to developers for technical support'.
contradictions.sentence_b: A user-visible message is written as one translatable string that holds entire sentences, with placeholder syntax for its variable parts (Thesis); its Limits exempt only 'Output that is ad hoc, local and aimed at other developers rather than end users, such as developer diagnostics'.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Where the project translates its user-facing text, the pinpointing message is one catalog message with the setting, its value and its location as placeholders; the rule asks what the message names, not how it is built.

contradictions.sentence_a: Example good half: `limit := flag.Int("max-body-kib", 512, "largest accepted request body in KiB, 1 to 10240; used only when -uploads is set")`.
contradictions.sentence_b: Text that a change adds for users to read, such as labels, prompts, status displays, help messages and error messages, is looked up from the project's resource or message catalog, by key or by passing it through the catalog's marking call, rather than handed to the code that displays it as a bare literal. The rule holds for a product that targets a single culture or region and for text written in English. (Thesis)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: The rule asks what the help text, documentation or message states; where the project keeps user-facing text in a catalog, the constraints are stated in the catalog entry.

gaps.concept: A calendar date or wall-clock time that names no moment (a birth date, a holiday, opening hours) is held in a local date or time type, never converted to an instant at midnight in UTC or the host's zone. The i18n note holds it 'held-cap — beyond max_rules 12'; TOOL-43's Limits only describe it ('A date or time that names no moment, such as a birth date, a holiday or an anniversary, is a floating value held in a plain date or date-time type with no offset or zone') and no card checks it.
gaps.source_path: w3c/timezone gh-pages index.html §'Floating Time Values' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/w3c/timezone/gh-pages/index.html), fetched by the research run and quoted in TOOL-43's Source; also dotnet/docs docs/core/extensions/globalization.md §'Serialization and time zone awareness' (fetched, per the i18n note)

gaps.concept: Dependencies are kept current through regular small updates (held-not-checkable: a property of the repository over time)
An update inside the declared range is verified by building and running the tests (held-not-checkable)
Code depends on the current head of its dependencies rather than on pinned versions (held-not-checkable: an organization's dependency model)
An option whose users choose among a few settings is a boolean or a small enumeration (held-not-checkable; the diff-visible case sits with an enumeration card outside the domain)
Configuration a deployment uses is kept in version control (held-not-checkable: repository layout)

A secret reaches the program through a protected file, a pipe or a secrets service, and through an environment variable only where the deployment offers none of these (held-not-checkable: a property of the platform)
The character set, the string types and where user-visible strings are kept are decided before construction (held-not-checkable: a design-time decision)

facet_errors.evidence: Thesis: 'An external package that a module's code imports or references directly is declared in that module's manifest' — a property of imports and manifest, not 'the shape, size and description of the change' (the taxonomy's review).
Thesis: 'every package imported by code that ships is declared as a runtime dependency' — a manifest property, not the change's shape, size or description.
Thesis: 'Each dependency the ecosystem's manifest declares carries a version requirement whose lower bound is the lowest version the code works with' — a manifest property.
Thesis: 'In the manifest of a package that other projects depend on, each runtime requirement admits more than one version' — a manifest property.

Thesis: 'A project that builds an application or service ... keeps under version control the lock file its package manager generates' — the repository's tracked files, not the change's shape, size or description.

Thesis: 'A dependency-install step in continuous integration, a container build or a deployment script installs from the ecosystem's committed lock file in the package manager's frozen mode' — a script property.
Thesis: 'the version that resolves carries no known advisory affecting code the project ships' — a property of the resolved version.
Thesis: 'A package added to the manifest for trivial functionality ... is taken only when it brings no packages of its own' — a dependency choice, not the change's shape.
Thesis: 'A package name that a change adds ... names the package the change intends to use' — the name's correctness, not the change's shape.
Thesis: 'A change to a build or check script keeps the build isolated from the host it runs on' — a property of the script.
Thesis: 'the change rewrites that code so the finding goes away' — how code is fixed, not the change's shape.
Thesis: 'Each suppression a change adds or edits ... carries a reason' — the content of a suppression.
Thesis: 'A failing or flaky test or check that a change does not fix stays in the suite under the test framework's skip, ignore or expected-failure mark' — how a test is disabled.
Thesis: 'every suppression names exactly the diagnostics it is meant to silence' — the content of a suppression.
Thesis: 'A suppression of a compiler or analyzer finding sits on the most deeply nested element where the language's suppression mechanism takes effect' — its placement in code.
Thesis: 'a suppression added by a change uses that form instead of the silent one' — the form of a suppression.
Thesis: 'An IP address, a URL or an absolute file path whose value differs between the environments ... is supplied at run time' — a property of code.
Thesis: 'A program defines its flags only in its entry point, and reads environment variables only there' — code structure.

Thesis: 'Each flag, environment variable or configuration key that a change exposes ... carries a setting with explicit semantics or visible external impact that users need to set' — a configuration-design decision.
Thesis: 'A secret such as a password, token or private key never reaches a process as a command-line argument' — a property of code.
Thesis: 'A debug mode ... is disabled for every component in production environments' — a code and configuration value.
Thesis: 'Each configuration option a change adds states its constraints in at least one form its users see' — option documentation.
Thesis: 'During initialisation ... the program reads, converts and checks each configuration setting it will use' — program behaviour.
Thesis: 'the program denies the setting and reports a message that pinpoints the error' — program behaviour.
Thesis: 'A value the user set for a configuration option ... is converted by a parser that reports unexpected characters, overflow and unrecognised words' — program behaviour.
Thesis: 'A configuration setting the program receives but does not apply produces a warning or an error' — program behaviour.
Thesis: 'A call that turns bytes into text or text into bytes ... names the encoding the data has' — a property of a call.
Thesis: 'Code that measures, indexes, slices or truncates a string is explicit about which view of the string it counts' — a property of code.
Thesis: 'Text meant to be interpreted independently of locale ... is case-mapped with the root locale' — a property of code.

Validator: 'read an entry whose requirement is declared elsewhere — a workspace root, a platform or bill of materials, a dependency constraint or a constraints file — at that declaration; a name with no version constraint states no lower bound only when no such declaration governs it' — other repository files.
Validator: 'confirm ... that the repository commits a lock file, or a manifest that fixes every version, for the manifest the step installs' — the repository's tracked files.

Validator: 'decide whether the path reaches a tool or input outside the checked-out tree, the build's managed tools and its explicit list of host tools ... and whether an output path of the step resolves inside the source tree'; Limits: an output directory 'that holds no version-controlled file' is outside the source tree — the host-tool list and the tracked files lie outside the hunk.

Validator: 'In the committed suppression baseline that the analyzer's configuration names, changed or not, check at head that entries for violations the change fixed or deleted are gone' — other files, not the base version of this path.

Validator: 'confirm that the project's toolchain, at every version it builds with, the oldest supported one included, offers a self-reporting form ... Open the project's analyzer configuration ... Open the suppression's reason and the build configuration the hunk belongs to'.

Validator: 'decide whether the read sits in the program's entry point, in a helper in the entry point's own module that only the entry point calls, or in the project's one configuration module ... Skip a variable on the project's documented allow-list' — the helper's callers, the configuration module and the allow-list lie outside the file.

Validator: 'trace each such failure to the message it produces, to where it is caught and to how the program ends. Check ... that the error reaches the entry point, and that the entry point reports it' — for 'a library that loads settings for its caller' (Limits) the entry point is another file.
Validator: 'read the hunk, its file and any declared minimum runtime version' — the declared minimum runtime version lives in build or package metadata, another file.

Validator: 'Check whether the literal already passes through the project's catalog lookup or marking call, and whether a recorded suppression covers the file'; Limits: 'a lint configuration that turns the hard-coded display-text check off for a folder and its subfolders'.

Validator: 'Open the build or packaging configuration and confirm that the shipped artifact receives its packages by installing the manifest's runtime list rather than carrying them in a bundle built in development; for a provided or peer entry, confirm whether the target environment or the host application supplies the package.'

Validator: 'establish whether the package is published for others to depend on ... or only builds an application or binary ... skip ... a cap or exclusion that a comment or linked issue ties to a known break or vulnerability.'

Validator: 'decide whether the project builds an application or service installed from this repository, or a package that other projects declare as a dependency; when those files leave the role undecided, do not flag.'
Validator: 'confirm that the step runs in an automated pipeline, that the job does not re-resolve only to test newer versions or to propose them as a reviewed change'.
Validator: 'trace the literal to its use, following a named constant to the lines that read it ... and whether the value would differ on another host, network or environment, test included.'

Validator: 'Read the file name, the format and the surrounding code for the encoding the data has' — the card's own bad Example (an ISO-8859-1 file read with read_to_string) is caught only by that judgement.
Validator: 'decide whether the text goes into a protocol, file, message or export format the change introduces, or into an existing format the change deploys in a new context'.
Validator: 'Open the hunk to decide whether the string reaches an end user ... or only developers ... Trace each operand'.

Validator: 'For each package an added import names, decide whether the importing file ships'; the bad Example's flagged line is the source import `import { parse } from "yamlx"; // src/config.ts, part of the shipped package`, and the Limits bound the rule by shipping ('Code that never ships imports development and test dependencies correctly'), not by file kind.

Thesis: 'When a change deletes or replaces the last code that uses a package, so that no source file, test, tool, build script, configuration file or platform-specific file of the project uses it any longer'; the finding quotes 'the deleted import line of the package' in source code.

Validator: 'Grep the hunk for added skip, ignore, disabled and expected-failure marks, rerun settings, ...'; Thesis: 'An automatic rerun ... a change that adds one carries the tracking issue as well'; its Source's Gradle Test Retry plugin sets reruns in the build.

Rationale: 'It also induces unnecessary maintenance: 22% of the dependency updates developers performed were made on bloated dependencies' and the package 'grows the built binary and increases maintenance effort' — a maintainability defect tied to measured cost.

Rationale: 'Parameters set in a configuration file that do not influence the runtime behaviour fail the user's intent ... 70.4% (19 of 27) happened without any system message or log' — measured failures; TOOL-30 rates the sibling silent overruling, from the same SOSP study, major.

Rationale: 'A meeting scheduled today for 13:00 next October 1, Dublin time, can be mis-handled after Ireland changes its daylight saving rules when the software relies on conversions made before the change' — a correctness failure, not a clarity or design cost; TOOL-43, on the same sources, is major.

Thesis: 'Options of one kind keep one case-sensitivity convention for their values, and one unit granularity unless each states its unit in its name or in a required value suffix'; Rationale: 'Inconsistent case sensitivity or unit granularity across parameters of the same type is error-prone' — a design cost (minor), which the Validator flags beside the documentation case.

trigger_errors.problem: does not match the bad Example: `# def test_import(): ...` is one comment line, the signal fires on 'two or more consecutive comment lines carrying statement syntax', and no regex trigger matches it, so the card reaches its bad Example only through `@pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=3)` (pattern `@flaky\b|\breruns\s*=|retryTimes\(|[.]retries\(`); a hunk that comments out one test is not dispatched

does not match the bad Example's defect: the bad half holds no configuration-file line, and the pattern matches only `cfg.BatchSize = 64`, a Go assignment inside the test that the Validator excludes ('in a configuration file the program ships or deploys with; skip comments and test fixtures')

summary: No two specific TOOL cards flag one line for one defect, but the always-on TOOL-13 duplicates ten of them whenever the project configures the analyzer rule they cite, so its DEFER_TO entry should grow from ['DOC-21', 'API-32'] to add TOOL-01, -15, -18, -20, -21, -22, -23, -26, -39 and -43 (eight more share the defect but quote a different span). Twelve contradictions: three in the rules (TOOL-13's false-positive-only marking vs TOOL-14's reasoned and temporary suppressions, TOOL-22's in-place read vs TOOL-23, TOOL-33's named locale encoding vs TOOL-34's UTF-8 new formats) and nine good-half Examples a sibling flags (allow vs expect, locale-default text I/O, environment reads, a one-word boolean parse, an uncaught conversion, untranslated help and error text). Facets: review on 29 cards whose Thesis concerns code, 9 scopes the Validator exceeds, 8 mechanical Validators that judge, 3 applies_to and 4 severities; triggers: TOOL-08 identical to TOOL-01, TOOL-10, TOOL-15 and TOOL-21 each nested in two siblings, TOOL-17 and TOOL-32 reaching their bad Examples only through incidental lines; gaps: floating dates and bidi or invisible source characters (held-cap) and CI action pinning, each with a GitHub-hosted source, plus 11 concepts held as not checkable.
